articles.title: B/R's Favorite 10 Sports Photos of All-Time
articles.summary: Photography has evolved just as rapidly as the rest of the digital world, but the goal has remained the same: Tell a story without saying a word. Sports photography, in particular, adds the challenge of capturing athletes and their biggest moments in motion.
articles.body:
Photography has evolved just as rapidly as the rest of the digital world, but the goal has remained the same: Tell a story without saying a word. Sports photography, in particular, adds the challenge of capturing athletes and their biggest moments in motion.

An iconic sports photo captures more than just a win or a loss. It can paint the picture of a career, define an entire era, or immerse you in a once-in-a-lifetime atmosphere.

All legendary sports photos have something in common, though: They're conveying one of the many emotions that make us love sports in the first place. Whether it's triumph, defeat, or the struggle in between, the best sports photos make you feel something.

The list of great sports photos is almost endless, but here are our 10 favorites of all time.

You're just not going to see a reasonable list of iconic sports photos that leaves off Muhammad Ali hovering over Sonny Liston after their title bout on May 25, 1965.

It's funny. The image captured by Neil Leifer didn't even make the cover of Sports Illustrated at the time. The moment itself wasn't particularly significant among Ali's many achievements – he'd already defeated Liston decisively before this rematch – yet the photo has become a lasting representation of Ali's career and impact.

The quality of the photo and the skill of the photographer are really what separate this from the thousands of other Ali photos and elevate it to legendary status. The angle, with larger-than-life Ali hovering over Liston (and all of us), has come to represent the man and his legacy better than words ever could. The beating of the chest, the bright lights, and Ali's roar all capture the charisma and fearlessness that have come to define his legacy.

Michael Jordan's Air Jordan Photo From the 1988 NBA Slam Dunk Contest

Michael Jordan is arguably (folks, please, we're not going there right now) the best NBA player of all time. He's got six rings, six Finals MVPs, and played the most important role on the Bulls' dynastic run. His accolades are plentiful, his iconic moments are abundant, and yet the greatest picture of him was captured in a dunk contest.

It was the 1988 Slam Dunk Contest at the All-Star game in Chicago. Of course, Jordan won – with a perfect score – in dramatic fashion. He famously took flight from the free-throw line; the picture by Bulls team photographer Bill Smith would not only epitomize Jordan's "Jumpman" nickname, but also serve as absurdly effective marketing for the Air Jordan shoe.

Jordan's greatness was fueled by a relentless competitiveness in all things. On the surface, the visual of him suspended in the air makes this picture special. But when you really think about it, it's also because -- not in spite -- of the fact that this was during a dunk contest. He treated every day like Game 7. This photo is a testament to his mentality.

Lou Gehrig Declares Himself "The Luckiest Man on the Face of the Earth"

It's hard to even look at this photo of Lou Gehrig announcing his retirement without getting teary-eyed.

It was July 4, 1939. "The Iron Horse" stood at home plate in his Yankees uniform, leaning into a sea of microphones to deliver his famous "Luckiest Man on the Face of the Earth" speech. Forced to retire due to ALS, the disease that he brought awareness to and that bears his name, Gehrig addressed more than 60,000 fans during "Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day" to thank them and share his gratitude for the game and his life in it.

"So I close in saying that I may have had a tough break, but I have an awful lot to live for," he ended.

The solemn day and photograph, as sad as they are, show the power of community that sports give us.

Tommie Smith and John Carlos Raise Their Fists in Protest at the 1968 Olympic Games

During the 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico City, U.S. sprinters Tommie Smith and John Carlos won gold and bronze in the 200-meter event. At the medal ceremony, they stood barefoot, wearing black gloves, and raised their fists during the U.S. national anthem.

The Olympics have long served as a reflection of the state of the world and its countries. It's an opportunity for the best athletes in the world to use the platform to stand up for what they believe in.

Smith and Carlos have called the gesture a "human rights" salute. It was carefully planned: They took off their shoes to draw attention to poverty, wore beads to recall lynch scenes, and raised their fists as a symbol of the struggle. The silent protest/gesture came just years after the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and months after the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.

The image became one of the most iconic images of the Black Panther Movement, which intended to end racial inequality in America.

Smith and Carlos faced backlash and consequences like expulsion from the Games at the time. Now, we look at this photo as one of the most overt protests in sports history. It involves two members of a nation representing that nation on the world stage while simultaneously reckoning with its past, present, and future. Smith and Carlos received an Arthur Ashe Courage Award at the 2008 ESPY Awards honoring their action.

Brandi Chastain Celebrates After USWNT Wins 1999 World Cup

Brandi Chastain's celebration of her 1999 World Cup clincher for Team USA is epic in and of itself, but it's fair to say the impact the photo had on women's soccer in the US was even greater.

It was USA vs. China in the final of the Women's World Cup in the Rose Bowl. After a goalless 120 minutes, the game went to a penalty shootout. Chastain took USA's fifth penalty. As the ball hit the lower right corner of the net, she tore off her jersey, knelt on the grass, and swung her jersey in the air in jubilation.

This was a groundbreaking moment for women's soccer and the sport's growth. Chastain became the figurative -- and literal -- poster child of it all. The image appeared on the cover of most sports magazines that week. In 2015, her Sports Illustrated cover was voted the second most iconic cover in the history of the magazine.

The entertainment factor of that World Cup, paired with the photo, inspired a new generation of girls to take an interest in the sport. Of course, the events on the field were enough to see a surge in popularity, but there's no doubt the photo was the perfect finishing touch to elevate the moment and put a face to the movement.

One of the greatest plays in baseball history, "The Catch" also remains up there with the greatest photographs in sports history.

A 12-time Gold Glove winner, Willie Mays made the most iconic defensive play of his career in Game 1 of the 1954 World Series. In the eighth inning, with the game tied 2-2, Mays made an improbable over-the-shoulder catch while running at full speed to record the out. Then, his throw back to the infield prevented one of the runners from advancing. From there, the Giants took the momentum, won Game 1 5-2 in extra innings, and went on to sweep Cleveland.

The beauty of this photo is in the crowd reaction. You can almost feel the silence as Mays is in the process of pulling it off. It was the perfect storm: a high-stakes situation, a legendary athlete making a legendary play, a stunned crowd, and the moment momentum shifted.

Wilt Chamberlain Scores 100 Points in an NBA Game

Did you know that this classic photograph of Wilt Chamberlain after the first (and only) 100-point night in NBA history was taken by a fan?

Yeah, there are unfortunately no highlights of Chamberlain's 100-point game, a record he set on March 2, 1962, that he still holds today. There were no official photographers in Hershey, PA, that night. The game wasn't televised. As legend has it, most New York sports reporters were at baseball spring training. The fan who took the photo, Paul Vathis, was actually a professional photojournalist who happened to be in attendance and would later win a Pulitzer Prize for an unrelated photo.

So how did they make do? Vathis realized history was unfolding at the end of the third quarter and ran to his car to get his camera. In the locker room after the final buzzer, Warriors PR professional Harvey Pollock grabbed a piece of paper, wrote "100" on it, and handed it to a seated Chamberlain.

This moment serves as a cautionary reminder that you never know when -- or where -- sports history is going to strike. The story behind the photo adds to the lore of the event itself. The sports history world is forever grateful for an off-duty Vathis among a crowd of fewer than 5,000 folks who witnessed the historic night.

Jesse Owens' Gold-Medal Ceremony at the 1936 Olympics

Berlin was hosting the Olympics during Hitler's reign in 1936. The Nazi regime set out to use the Games for propaganda and a showcase of Aryan supremacy, but African American track athlete Jesse Owens had other plans.

Owens won four gold medals and set three world records against a backdrop of swastikas and Nazi salutes, defying Hitler's agenda all around him.

This moment transcended sports and reflected the pre-World War II Era. While the USA's decision to attend the Berlin Olympics was controversial, Owens' dominance was a bright spot. The bravery and prowess of an extraordinary athlete and man lives on forever in this photo.

Great photography skills, high stakes, an iconic moment, and a legendary player combined to give us the photo every hockey fan thought of when clicking on this article. There's a reason this one has been turned into a statue outside of TD Garden. They don't do that for just anyone in Boston.

Bobby Orr's "The Goal" depicts Orr scoring the game-winner for the Bruins against the Blues in overtime of Game 4 of the 1970 Stanley Cup Final.

An elated Orr saw the puck slip into the net and jumped into the air with joy, but opponent Noel Picard had hooked his stick, causing him to hover over the ice as if he were flying. He then flew right into the arms of his teammates as he lifted his Bruins to their first title in 29 years.

It's now simply known as "the goal" for many reasons, including the timing of the now-iconic picture taken by Ray Lussier. Lussier has told some great stories about behind-the-scenes from the night .

Michael Phelps' Photo Finish Win at the 2008 Summer Olympics

Few iconic photos in sports history actually influenced the event in the photo, but Michael Phelps' win over Serbian swimmer Milorad Čavić by 0.01 seconds at the 2008 Summer Olympics is one of them.

The 100-meter butterfly final was one of the closest calls in Olympic swimming history, requiring video slowed to one frame per 10,000th of a second to declare Phelps the winner. To the naked eye, it seemed like Cavic touched first because he was already reaching for the wall, but Phelps was just a fraction of a second quicker.

The stakes were ridiculously high, as Phelps tied the record for seven golds in a single Olympics with the win. He'd go on to break the record with eight.

articles.title: Rand Paul: Politicians should stay out of college sports and let athletes compete freely
articles.summary: Sen. Rand Paul argues that politicians, not the NCAA, should decide college sports rules, athlete compensation, transfers and conference membership.
articles.body: The people who oversee the Post Office now want to run college sports ... what could go wrong? The United States Congress has been called upon during the most important moments in American history to make difficult decisions about the future of our country. We have navigated wars, economic downturns and national disasters. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! These are the kinds of nationwide issues that a federal government should address. The Founders never intended for the federal government to usurp the authority of your local school board or your homeowners’ association. I don’t think it ever occurred to them that Congress would one day be charged with dictating the rules for college sports. And yet, with gas at over $4 a gallon, a persistent war with Iran and $40 trillion in debt, the Senate decided the most urgent thing it should do is dictate how college sports are run from Washington. It came to this decision, of course, after acknowledging that government caused the very problems this bill purports to fix. This is the exact scenario the great Harry Browne described when he said government "knows how to break your legs, then hand you a crutch and say, ‘See, if it weren’t for government, you wouldn’t be able to walk.’" I come to the floor today to offer an amendment that would avoid the federal takeover of college sports. Unlike the underlying bill, my amendment rejects the idea that politicians should run college sports. My amendment would put the trust in the schools, students, coaches and conferences to run their own sports. My amendment accomplishes this goal simply by granting an antitrust exemption so that college athletes and schools can make their own deals, without unelected judges or politicians micromanaging every detail of compensation and eligibility. Jason Russell, a journalist with Reason magazine perhaps summed up this bill’s federal takeover of college sports best when he wrote: "The backers of the bill believe politicians, not the NCAA, should decide how many transfers are allowed. They think politicians, not conferences, should set a compensation cap on how much schools can pay athletes. They think politicians, not athletes and businesses, should get to decide what is a legitimate private contract. They think politicians, not the colleges, should decide how many schools are in the Big Ten and SEC. They think politicians, not coaches, should decide when a coach is allowed to leave a job. "They think politicians, not athletes or agents, should get to decide what agent fees are. They think politicians should empower medical personnel, not athletes or coaches, to have "autonomous, unchallengeable" power to decide if an athlete plays or sits. "They even think politicians, not the NFL or broadcasters, should get to decide when professional football games are on TV. They think politicians should have a say in the length of the college football season." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE This bill is the culmination of a slow march towards federal control of college sports that began almost one-hundred and forty years ago in the courts. In 1890, Congress enacted the Sherman Act. The Sherman Act is a piece of antitrust legislation. But, quite quickly, antitrust became a weapon against businesses of all sizes. One of the most ridiculous examples of antitrust as a weapon of government control came in 1967. In Utah Pie Company v. Continental Baking Company, the courts determined that a bakery violated antitrust law by selling its pies too cheaply. Not long after, in 1969, the government sued IBM for dominating the computer market by innovating too quickly. That case ultimately ran on for thirteen years before the government finally dropped it, saying that it was "without merit." The logic of antitrust became so contorted that the Federal Trade commission accused cereal makers of maintaining a shared monopoly on the theory that the brands blocked competition by being so popular that they flooded store shelves with their products. After 10 years of litigation, the FTC dismissed the case, ruling that staff failed to prove the shared monopoly charges. Antitrust laws granted the courts the ability to intrude on private contracts and dictate how people should run their businesses. And courts have grown increasingly comfortable using that power, increasing the scope of antitrust law with each case. For over one-hundred years this country has left regulation of college sports where it belongs: with the institutions and individuals that participate in college athletics. Until 1984, college athletics were excluded from antitrust law because antitrust didn’t deal with noncommercial, amateur pursuits. But in 1984 the Supreme Court decided that the NCAA couldn’t impose television broadcasting restrictions on college football games. Rather than recognizing that there may have been an underlying reason for the restrictions, the courts threw out the restrictions and began the slippery path we are on today. That case established college athletics as a commercial enterprise, but it wasn’t until 2015 that the courts really sank their fangs into college athletics. In 2015, the courts finally decided that the NCAA could not require students to maintain their amateur status by refusing payment for use of their name, image and likeness. The court decided that eligibility rules for a private association are best decided by the government, not the members of the association. Since 2015, a flurry of cases has decided issues as parochial as how much individual athletes are paid out of broadcast revenues and how long student athletes are eligible to play. Government has shirked its real duties — deciding issues of national importance — to focus on something it knows nothing about. As important as college sports are to students and institutions, they aren’t something Congress should micromanage. Athletes and institutions should be free to make choices about who they want to work and play for, and what rules they should be subject to. This bill manages to interfere with college athletics at nearly every level. It limits the ability of certain employees to freely leave one school and accept a job at another. It decides how students may go about licensing their name, image, and likeness. It even decides when transfer students are eligible to play. The bill actually forbids a return to the historic model of amateur sports where athletes are not paid. The bill would also set up a Commission on the Future of College Athletics, a legislative commission that would recommend new rule changes to Congress in the future. It seems that we already have an institution dedicated to preserving the future of college sports: the NCAA. Congress should not mire itself in another endless cycle of solving problems it caused. It especially shouldn’t become the chief rulemaking body for something like collegiate athletics. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That is why I am offering an amendment that would actually solve the problems faced by college sports. My amendment would reverse previous interference and prevent future interference by exempting collegiate sports from antitrust laws. This would ensure conferences, colleges and athletes are free to negotiate and enter into agreements that benefit everyone, without the heavy hand of government dictating what parties can offer or accept. It would also prevent Congress from imposing rules governing such minutiae as eligibility for transfer students and the thresholds for reporting name, image and likeness income. I love college sports as much as anyone, which is why I think the best way we can protect college sports is to stop sticking our nose where it doesn’t belong.

articles.title: 10.09 national record, a difficult season and now the Asian Games: Gurindervir Singh’s 100m test
articles.summary: “For me, the medal is the most important thing at the Asian Games.” Gurindervir Singh said that two weeks ago.
articles.body: “For me, the medal is the most important thing at the Asian Games.”Gurindervir Singh said that two weeks ago. Today, he gets his first chance to back it up.The Indian sprinter will begin his Asian Games 2026 campaign in the men's 100m today alongside compatriot Animesh Kujur, who has raced Gurindervir repeatedly this season.Gurindervir arrives at the Games after a season in which the results have not always matched the expectations created by his national record.In Glasgow at the Commonwealth Games in July, he ran 10.39 seconds in his 100m heat. He finished second in the race but did not advance to the semifinals, ending the competition 28th overall.There was another 10.39s in Bhubaneswar on August 22 at the World Athletics Continental Tour Silver meet in Bhubneshwar, where Gurindervir finished seventh in the final. Animesh was fifth with 10.32s.By the time the two Indians met again in Delhi on September 10, Gurindervir had moved to 10.32s; however, it was still not enough to beat Animesh, who won with a timing of 10.21s.Naturally, Gurindervir was not satisfied.“I am not satisfied with the timing, but yes, I found some parts of the race to be strong. I was very strong in the last 80 or 60 metres. The start was a little weak for me. Maybe I couldn't take the start well. My block exit wasn't good,” he had told TimesofIndia.com after the race.The final part of the race had also been an area his coach wanted him to work on, particularly the last 20 metres.“Yes, I will always have to work on it. Till the time I play, there will always be a chance for improvement. As the coach said, I have to work on the last 20 metres. So, I have 2-2.5 weeks before the Asian Games. I have training sessions. So, as the race comes closer, it will automatically get better,” Gurindervir had said.From 10.39s in Glasgow to 10.32s in Delhi: Gurindervir’s Asian Games build-upThose two weeks have now passed, and the 25-year-old said his preparation after the Commonwealth Games had involved work away from the race itself.“I have improved a lot after the Commonwealth Games in terms of physique, weight training, track and endurance. I have tried to improve everything, and it has been done.”He had also been clear about where the Asian Games sat in his plans.“The main race is the Asian Games. The final target is the Asian Games,” he said.The other number attached to Gurindervir's campaign is 10.09s - the national record he set in May at the National Senior Athletics Championships in Ranchi.‘Let it happen at the Asian Games’: Gurindervir on the sub-10 barrierThe season best is also his personal best, and the next barrier or goal, rather, is obvious. Gurindervir has spoken about breaking 10 seconds, but when asked about its possibility, he hoped it might happen at Aichi-Nagoya.“If it happens, let it happen at the Asian Games.”“Because the timing is coming in training. They [support team] graph it. They show the timing that it can happen. So, I will have to try again and again. I will have to run the race. When I run, the time will improve. And then I will run below 10.”But he also left room for the race itself to decide whether that happens. “When we get good races, and the conditions are good, I will run well. My body will feel fully reactive. So, it can happen that day.”The Asian Games will provide a different test from the domestic races that have occupied much of his season. Gurindervir is not convinced the leading sprinters in Asia are beyond his reach.The medal is the most important thing’: Gurindervir faces Asia’s bestThe field includes Japan's Yuki Koike, who has a 9.98s PB and Shuhei Tada (10.01s), while Thailand's Puripol Boonson has ran 9.94s. China's Xie Zhenye, the former Asian champion, owns a 9.97s PB and Iran's Hassan Taftian has run 10.03s. Gurindervir's 10.09 national record puts him in that group, with Animesh’s at 10.14s.“They have run well, and we are also running well,” he said.“[It will depend on] whose day it is, who is feeling good, whose body is running. Anything can happen. We cannot predict 100 metres.”He added: “It's not like they are extraordinarily strong and we are far behind them. There is a slight difference of one or two micro-points. So, we don't even know who is ahead and who is behind.”Animesh's presence in the same event has been a constant through the season for Gurindervir, but he does not see their competition as a distraction.“It is a healthy thing. I think it is happening in Athletics; more people have started looking at athletics with interest. It is good for us too. He gets the motivation, I get the motivation. We train better, and there is a focus on training. We are consistent. So, it is a good thing.”The 10.09 national record is already his. The sub-10 mark is still there. But when he was asked what he wanted from the Asian Games, he was not focused on the timing.“For me, the medal is the most important thing at the Asian Games. Timing is important. If we run well, we will get the medal. But I have worked very hard for the medal for the whole year, and I am still working on it. I will do my best to win the medal and finish on the podium.”Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Japan’s Ohashi breaks 200m breaststroke world record at Asian Games
articles.summary: Shin Ohashi, 17, claims his second Asian Games gold with his record-breaking effort in front of a thrilled home crowd.
articles.body:
Japan’s 17-year-old swimmer Shin Ohashi has broken the men’s 200-metre breaststroke world record on the way to Asian Games gold and soaked up the moment in front of a thrilled home crowd.

Ohashi’s blistering time of two minutes and 4.83 seconds at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre on Thursday eclipsed the previous record of 2:05.48, set by China’s Qin Haiyang at the 2023 World Aquatics Championships in Fukuoka, Japan.

“The world record was my goal, so I’m very happy to get it,” he said.

“Thanks to my fans, my family, all who supported me.

“My next goal is for the gold medal at the world championships.”

Kazakhstan’s Denis Petrashov finished 3.84 seconds behind Ohashi to claim silver ahead of South Korean Cho Sung-jae (2:08.76).

“There was a strong rival in the breaststroke. It went exactly as I had thought,” Cho said of Ohashi.

“Honestly, I never imagined a world record would come out of it. I am delighted to come away with a medal.”

Ohashi’s triumph came days after French swimmer Leon Marchand, the Olympic 200m breaststroke champion, praised the Japanese swimmer and called him a major threat.

“I’m scared. I’m very scared of him,” Marchand said of Ohashi.

“He’s still so young. His coach is really good. I think his entourage, the people around him, are really good, so I hope he’s going to keep improving.”

Thursday’s medal adds to the 100m breaststroke gold Ohashi shared with China’s Dong Zhihao (58.64) ahead of Games record holder Qin, who settled for bronze. He also powered Japan to silver in both the men’s and mixed 4x100m medley relays.

Ohashi could win his fifth and final medal on Friday in the 50m breaststroke.

articles.title: Buy or Sell These 8 WWE Stars Ever Winning a World Championship
articles.summary: A world championship isn't always in the cards for even WWE's most promising prospects.
articles.body:
A world championship isn't always in the cards for even WWE's most promising prospects.

Some of the biggest names to grace WWE's squared circle were never able to win the prestigious prize. From Roddy Piper to Mr. Perfect, it always eluded them for one reason or another.

The roster being as star-studded as it was when they were at the peak of their popularity was the primary reason for them being snubbed, and WWE suffers from a similar issue today. Having two top titles for the men between Raw and SmackDown makes it more attainable, but there's no guarantee that everyone waiting in the wings for an opportunity will get their turn.

Nonetheless, the potential of certain Superstars can't be ignored, and it's more a matter of when than if they'll be wearing world title gold around their waist. This is, of course, barring any serious injuries or drastic changes in their booking.

Which of the eight athletes have a WWE world championship in their future?

Oba Femi was destined to win a world championship in WWE from the moment he made his main roster debut at the onset of 2026.

A two-time NXT champion, Femi's domination of the NXT landscape made it clear that he'd have a high ceiling once he hit Raw or SmackDown. Sure enough, he immediately made an enemy out of Brock Lesnar, who he soundly defeated not once but twice on pay-per-view.

Femi had the chance to challenge for a world title at SummerSlam by virtue of becoming King of the Ring back in June, but opted to forgo the title shot so he could face Lesnar inside Hell in a Cell at the event instead. It's hardly been acknowledged since, so it's safe to assume that the opportunity is no longer on the table.

All signs point to him being the one to dethrone Roman Reigns for the World Heavyweight Championship at WrestleMania 43, which would mean a Royal Rumble victory is almost a certainty. Whether he wins it or not, he'll find his way into the world title match at 'Mania and emerge with the gold in his grasp.

Two weeks ago, it didn't look like Penta would ever be a world champion in WWE.

For as over with the audience as he is and for as much success as he's had since joining the promotion in early 2025, he was never utilized as anything other than an upper-midcard competitor. That was, however, until he earned the opportunity to fight Roman Reigns for the World Heavyweight Championship in his native Mexico on Raw.

The match was so great that it may have just changed the trajectory of his entire career. The crowd that night was wildly behind the masked marvel and he more than proved he can hang at an elite level.

WWE wisely followed up on his hot momentum on the Sept. 21 edition of Raw by having him cut a promo to start the show and then qualify for the men's Money in the Bank Ladder match at the end of it. Dominik Mysterio was one of the favorites to capture the briefcase, so Penta advancing over him might be a case of WWE changing plans.

If so, Penta becoming Mr. Money in the Bank would be his ticket to eventually winning a world title. He wouldn't necessarily need to cash in on Reigns, but it would be a waste to give him the contract if he was going to fall short for a second straight time.

The electric reaction to Penta in Mexico City had to have convinced the company that they'd be leaving money on the table if they didn't put a world championship on him at some point.

Royce Keys is in the midst of the biggest push of his career as the leader of the new 946 stable on Raw.

He's had a great first year in WWE in general by debuting in the men's Royal Rumble match, winning the Andre the Giant Memorial Battle Royal and being slotted into a top storyline on Raw with The Bloodline.

He showed real upside in AEW and held a handful of titles, but he was never able to get beyond a certain level. He might end up being more of a mainstay in the main event scene in WWE than he was in AEW, but his chances of winning a world title are equally slim.

He will run into the same problem that plagued him in AEW, and that's being overshadowed by the bigger shows. He's an exciting opponent for Reigns, but once he loses, his faction will fizzle out and he'll settle into a midcard role on the show.

That's a perfectly fine spot for him, but he is capable of more. WWE has done an excellent job of portraying him as a force to be reckoned with as of late, but there's been nothing else to suggest that they intend to build around him as the centerpiece of either Raw or SmackDown in the long haul.

Even with all eyes on Oba Femi at the moment, Bron Breakker shouldn't be overlooked as a future face of WWE.

That's been the basis of their ongoing rivalry, and it's something Breakker continues to struggle with. Femi stole a lot of thunder when he was called up earlier in the year, while Breakker's booking hasn't quite been the same since he was sidelined with an injury.

Despite that, Breakker will get to the upper echelon of WWE before long. It doesn't appear it will happen as soon as it will for Femi, but he has all the tools to be a big star for many years to come.

He unsuccessfully challenged CM Punk for the World Heavyweight Championship on Raw's premiere episode of 2026. That would have been as good of a time as any for him to be crowned champ, but WWE waiting just a little longer will make that moment all the more monumental when it comes to fruition in the next year or so.

The Vision started out as a compelling concept when crashed onto the scene in the spring of 2025, but they never truly found their footing before Seth Rollins had to be pulled due to an injury he sustained that October.

It's been a series of unfortunate events since then with Bron Breakker, Bronson Reed and Logan Paul all getting hurt at different points and ruining anything The Vision could get going.

Reed recently returned and has looked better than ever before, begging the question of whether WWE would actually go all the way with him and make him a world champ down the road. The answer is most likely not, and that applies to Paul as well.

Paul becoming a full-timer for WWE a year ago increased his chances of one day winning a world title, but he simply hasn't shown that he's worthy of wearing the gold. He's good for the occasional spectacle in the ring, but otherwise, he's far better off as a supporting player in the midcard.

WWE ever putting the top title on him would reek of desperation, and while it's not completely out of the realm of possibility, whatever mainstream attention they'd get out of it wouldn't be worth it.

Trick Williams was one of those NXT call-ups whose eventual success was undeniable based on the decorated stint he had down in developmental.

He held the NXT Championship on two occasions as well as the TNA World Championship, so he's no stranger to holding gold. He quickly clinched the United States Championship within months of signing to SmackDown and has had a recurring role on the show ever since.

Williams is fresh off regaining the star-spangled prize from Baron Corbin at Sunday Night's Main Event, so there's no need to rush him into the main event picture, but he does find himself involved in the upcoming men's Money in the Bank Ladder match. Williams walking around with that briefcase in his possession would be a natural sight.

That said, it'd be premature to put him toward the top of the card anytime soon. He remains a work in progress in the ring and needs to further flesh out his character, but with the way he's been used so far, WWE certainly sees him as a world champion-caliber competitor and rightfully so.

Dominik Mysterio's 2025 was nothing short of stellar, but his 2026 has sadly been anything but. He lost his feud to Finn Bálor, dropped the AAA Mega Championship to El Grande Americano, failed to qualify for Money in the Bank and, worst of all, came up short against Danhausen at SummerSlam.

WWE has lost their way with Mysterio for whatever reason, yet he will win a world championship someday, nonetheless.

His evolution both as a character and as an in-ring performer has been spectacular to see over the last six years, and he's still featured fairly frequently on Raw as a member of The Judgment Day. At this point, the group is doing more to hold him back than build him up, so a split from the stable should be imminent.

He's also been a heel for so long that he could benefit big time from a babyface turn when the time comes. However, it'd be more fitting for him to win his first world title as a dastardly heel, ideally through the use of the Money in the Bank briefcase.

On paper, Mysterio as either Undisputed WWE or World Heavyweight champion sounds comical currently, but at only 29-years-old, he still has his whole career ahead of him to make it happen.

LA Knight will finally get his crack at the World Heavyweight Championship against Roman Reigns at Money in the Bank on Oct. 10, and it's perhaps the best chance he's ever had at winning a world title in WWE.

That makes it all the more frustrating that he isn't leaving with the prestigious prize.

Knight has been ready for a run with the top title since debuting on the main roster four years ago, not to mention he endeared himself to the audience in record time. If WWE saw him as being at the main event level, he would have won a world title by now.

It really is now or never for Knight, who is rapidly approaching 44-years-old and is in jeopardy of being pushed aside in favor of the younger stars. It'd be an incredible occasion if he were to win the big one, and maybe WWE will throw him a bone if only so he can have the distinction of being a former world champ, but any fans automatically expecting it are setting themselves up for disappointment.

By never capturing a world championship, Knight will go down as one of WWE's biggest missed opportunities.

Graham Mirmina, aka Graham "GSM" Matthews, has specialized in sports and entertainment writing since 2010. Visit his website, WrestleRant , and subscribe to his YouTube channel for more wrestling-related content.

articles.title: 1 Player on Every NHL Team to Get Excited About Ahead of the 2026-27 Season
articles.summary: The NHL offseason ended last week when the 32 clubs opened their training camp. With the league's expanded 84-game schedule, the Sept. 29 puck drop for the 2026-27 regular season is only days away.
articles.body:
The NHL offseason ended last week when the 32 clubs opened their training camp. With the league's expanded 84-game schedule, the Sept. 29 puck drop for the 2026-27 regular season is only days away.

A new season always brings hope for players and fans of every club. Stanley Cup contenders believe that this is the year they win hockey's holy grail. Playoff contenders dream of taking the next step toward a championship, while rebuilding clubs try to break through as postseason teams.

Fans of every NHL team will look to one player to stoke their hopes for improvement. It could be an established superstar, a player with the potential to become an elite player, or a promising youngster.

Here's our take on one player on every NHL team to get excited about this season.

The rebuilding Anaheim Ducks made significant strides last season, qualifying for the playoffs for the first time since 2017-18 and upsetting the Edmonton Oilers in the first round. Left winger Cutter Gauthier led their offensive attack.

Gauthier is part of the Ducks' young core that includes playmaking center Leo Carlsson and sophomore winger Beckett Sennecke. He enjoyed a breakout sophomore season, leading the Ducks with 41 goals and 69 points in the regular season . He was also their postseason leader with 12 points.

At 6'2" and 205 pounds, the 21-year-old Gauthier is quickly becoming one of the NHL's top power forwards. He can also play center, doesn't shy away from physical play, and his hard, accurate shot could put him within range of 50 goals this season.

After missing the playoffs in 2024-25, the Boston Bruins rebounded last season with 100 points to earn a wild-card spot . David Pastrňák played a major role in the Bruins' bounce-back performance.

Pastrňák, 30, is among the league's elite scoring forwards. The Bruins right winger scored 100 points last season, finishing among the league's top-10 scorers . He also became the third player in Bruins history with at least four 100-point seasons.

The Bruins are hoping to build on last season's performance. With Pastrňák still in his prime, they have a good chance to do so. Few skaters can match his combination of shooting power, skating, and offensive instincts.

After 14 long seasons , the Buffalo Sabres finally ended their playoff drought last season. With established stars like Tage Thompson and Rasmus Dahlin and promising players like Josh Doan, Noah Östlund, Konsta Helenius, and Zach Benson, the Sabres are an emerging force in the Eastern Conference.

Of their young players, the 21-year-old Benson has emerged as one to watch. A pesky sparkplug winger, the 5'10", 178-pound left winger had 43 points in 65 games last season. He proved his worth in his first NHL postseason, finishing fourth among the Sabres playoff scorers with nine points in 13 games.

Benson's two-way skills and his energetic, agitating style earned him a seven-year contract with a $7.5 million AAV. A fan favorite in Buffalo, his production will continue to improve as he gains experience.

After barely missing the playoffs in 2024-25 , the Flames plunged toward the bottom of the standings last season. Management continued shipping out veterans as it pursued its rebuilding plan, putting faith in the youngsters they drafted or acquired through trades.

Matvei Gridin could be the youngster who brings some excitement to weary Flames fans. A 2024 first-round pick, the 20-year-old winger is a talented offensive forward with an accurate shot and strong playmaking skills. He's projected to be among the Flames' top-six forwards this season.

Called up by the Flames in January, the 6'1", 182-pound Gridin had 20 points in 37 games. If he builds on that promising effort this season, the Flames could have a budding offensive star on their hands.

Acquired from the Dallas Stars in last year's Mikko Rantanen trade, Logan Stankoven played a crucial role in the Carolina Hurricanes' march to the 2026 Stanley Cup. Centering the second line between wingers Taylor Hall and Jackson Blake, the 23-year-old led the Hurricanes with 11 postseason goals.

Stankoven and his linemates gave the Hurricanes an invaluable second-line scoring punch that had been missing in previous seasons. The 5'8", 165-pounder is a small but versatile forward, capable of playing center or wing. He proved that he could handle the wear and tear of playoff hockey.

Coming off a career-high 44-point performance, Stankoven should be more productive this season. His energetic, hard-working style and quick release will continue to make him difficult for opponents to contain.

With young superstar captain Connor Bedard sidelined to start the season, Chicago will look to Frank Nazar and rookie Anton Frondell to carry the load at center. This could give the 19-year-old Frondell a great opportunity to prove his worth early in his NHL career.

Chosen third overall in the 2025 NHL Draft, Frondell made his big-league debut late last season. He showed plenty of promise with nine points in 12 games, and could be up for the challenge of playing as their second-line center when this season begins.

The 6'1", 198-pound Frondell is a physical, competitive two-way forward with the versatility to play center or wing. He plays a style similar to Florida Panthers center Aleksander Barkov. If that ability shines through this season, he could become a serious contender for the Calder Memorial Trophy .

Led by center Nathan MacKinnon and defenseman Cale Makar, the Colorado Avalanche dominated the standings last season, finishing with a league-leading 121 points and their first Presidents' Trophy since 2020-21.

Makar has established himself as the league's top defenseman and a superstar in his own right, but MacKinnon remains the Avs most exciting player. The 31-year-old center reached the 100-point mark last season (127 points) for the fourth straight season, while his 53 goals earned him his first Maurice Richard Trophy .

Since 2022-23, only Edmonton's Connor McDavid and Tampa Bay's Nikita Kucherov have more total points than MacKinnon. He will remain a contender for the scoring title as the Avalanche attempt to bring the Stanley Cup back to Colorado for the first time since 2022.

For the second straight year, Zach Werenski was the Columbus Blue Jackets' best player. He led them in scoring with 81 points , one less than his team-leading (and career-best) 82-point performance in 2024-25. His efforts made him the first Blue Jackets defenseman to win the James Norris Memorial Trophy .

That award capped a difficult season for Werenski and his teammates. Their inconsistency cost them a playoff berth. In June, it was reported that the 29-year-old defenseman would welcome a trade. He was nearly shipped to the Dallas Stars, but insisted on staying to help the Blue Jackets win.

Despite the offseason turmoil, Werenski remains the Blue Jackets' top star and their best hope for ending their six-year playoff drought. An elite puck-moving defenseman in his prime, he will take on more of a leadership role this season.

After reaching the Western Conference Final in three straight years , the Stars were eliminated in the first round last season. To get back on track, they'll look to core players like Wyatt Johnston to lead the way.

Despite the Stars' early postseason exit, Johnston continued to blossom into a first-line center . The 23-year-old had his best season to date, finishing with a career-high 45 goals and 41 assists for 86 points to finish second among the Stars' leading scorers . He also had six points in as many playoff games.

The 6'1", 187-pound Johnston is a smart two-way player who has yet to reach his full potential. Signed through 2029-30 with an $8.5 million AAV, he will remain a crucial part of their lineup as they transition away from older Stars like Tyler Seguin and team captain Jamie Benn.

The Detroit Red Wings have endured inconsistency over the past three seasons, which stretched their playoff drought to 10 years. While that's resulted in front-office turmoil and uncertainty about the future of former captain Dylan Larkin, a bright spot remains star defenseman Moritz Seider.

Since being chosen sixth overall by the Red Wings in the 2019 NHL Draft, Seider has steadily developed into an elite all-around defenseman. He won the Calder Memorial Trophy in 2021-22 and has become the anchor of the Red Wings' blue line.

Seider, 25, is a workhorse who logs big minutes in all situations. He had a league-leading 2104:39 of total time on ice per game last season and a career-high 60 points. The young German is entering his prime and remains crucial to the Wings' hopes of ending their long postseason drought.

Entering his 12th NHL season, Connor McDavid continues to outshine all current NHL superstars. He proved it again last season by leading the league with 90 assists and 138 points to earn the Art Ross Trophy for the sixth time, tying him for second all-time with Hall of Famers Mario Lemieux and Gordie Howe.

The 29-year-old McDavid also won the Ted Lindsay Award for the fifth time, tying him with Wayne Gretzky for first place in that category. In the prime of his career, the Edmonton Oilers captain could continue adding to his trophy case this season.

McDavid is still pursuing his first Stanley Cup to cement his legacy among the game's greatest players. Given that motivation, he should continue to dazzle NHL fans with his impressive offensive skills.

An injury-filled season resulted in the Florida Panthers missing the playoffs for the first time since 2018-19. They'll attempt to return to Stanley Cup contender status this season with a healthier roster, buoyed by the addition of winger Brady Tkachuk.

The 26-year-old Tkachuk was acquired from the Ottawa Senators in June, joining his older brother Matthew on the same NHL team for the first time. They won't be on the same line to start the season, but it's only a matter of time before they do.

A pugnacious power forward, Tkachuk should fit in well with the Panthers' aggressive physical style. He'll also bring a welcome shot of youth, energy, and scoring to their talented but aging roster.

The retirement of long-time Los Angeles Kings first-line center Anze Kopitar leaves a big hole on their forward lines. It provides Quinton Byfield with a big opportunity to establish himself in that role .

Chosen second overall by the Kings in the 2020 NHL Draft, all eyes will be on the 24-year-old Byfield. A big power forward who can play center or wing, the 6'5", 230-pounder has had three seasons with 20-plus goals and between 49 and 55 points, but Kings fans await his big breakout season.

Byfield will get that chance this season. With his big frame, puck-handling ability, and two-way skills, he has the physical tools to become a dominant center. This could be the year he finally puts it all together.

This season will be Quinn Hughes' first full campaign with the Minnesota Wild since being acquired from the Vancouver Canucks last December. His addition last season helped the Wild reach their fourth-best regular season (104 points) and win their first playoff round since 2015.

An elite puck-moving defenseman, Hughes won the James Norris Memorial Trophy in 2023-24. Given his impressive offensive skills, he could add a second Norris Trophy to his mantle. He and Brock Faber give the Wild one of the league's best defensive pairings .

Hughes' eligibility for unrestricted free-agent status next July has raised uncertainty about his future in Minnesota. Nevertheless, his play this season could turn the Wild into a true Stanley Cup contender.

Four years after finishing last in the NHL standings, the Montreal Canadiens reached the Eastern Conference Final last season. Promising winger Ivan Demidov played a key role in his club's impressive improvement.

A creative puck-handling winger with terrific vision and hockey smarts, the 20-year-old Demidov led all rookies with 63 points last season, finishing as runner-up for the Calder Memorial Trophy . He will continue to play a significant role for the Canadiens during his sophomore campaign.

The Canadiens have a bevy of young stars like Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson, and Juraj Slafkovsky. However, Demidov could be the best natural talent of the bunch. He's only scratched the surface of his potential.

The Nashville Predators are under new management for the second time in three years, as former Colorado Avalanche GM Chris MacFarland took over the role in June. He has been retooling the roster, focusing on promising players like Matthew Wood.

Filip Forsberg, Roman Josi, and Steven Stamkos are well-known veterans, but Wood is part of the Predators' next generation of potential stars. The 21-year-old is coming off a promising 17-goal, 30-point rookie campaign. He could see more playing time since winger Luke Evangelista was traded to New Jersey.

At 6'4" and 202 pounds, Wood is a big power forward who could blossom into a dangerous scoring winger for the Predators. He's a pure goal scorer with a quick release who uses his size and reach to generate scoring chances.

Injuries continued to plague Jack Hughes last season, which contributed to the New Jersey Devils missing the playoffs. The talented 25-year-old center appeared in 61 games but still led his club with 77 points.

Hughes is a game-changing franchise player with outstanding offensive skills. He's already proven his capabilities when healthy. In 2022-23, he set the Devils' single-season franchise record with 99 points while leading his club to a franchise-record 112-point campaign.

A healthy Hughes could lead the Devils back into playoff contention this season. He's entering his prime and could break his own franchise points record.

Chosen first overall by the New York Islanders in the 2025 NHL Draft, Matthew Schaefer wasted little time establishing himself as a superstar. Skating on the top defense pairing, he finished with 23 goals and 59 points 82 games.

It was an astounding rookie performance, making Schaefer the youngest player to win the Calder Memorial Trophy. He also became the first to win by unanimous vote since Hall of Fame winger Teemu Selanne in 1992-93.

A highly skilled puck-moving defenseman, Schaefer is the foundation piece for the retooling Islanders. The 6'2", 186-pounder has the potential to become as great a defenseman as Islanders Hall of Famer Denis Potvin.

Despite the New York Rangers' poor performance last season, Igor Shesterkin reminded everyone he remains among the NHL's best goalies regardless of the team in front of him. The 30-year-old goalie finished among the league leaders with a 2.50 goals-against average and a .912 save percentage.

In his seven NHL seasons, Shesterkin has been the one constant for the Rangers, who've gone from winning the Presidents' Trophy in 2023-24 to finishing near the bottom of the standings two years later. His consistency and clutch play has put him among the league's top goalies.

Winner of the Vezina Trophy in 2021-22, Shesterkin will be relied on to provide the retooling Rangers with the steady netminding necessary to return to playoff contention. With an improved roster in front of him this season, he'll give the Blueshirts a chance to win every game he starts.

The Ottawa Senators head into this season trying to put the offseason departure of former captain Brady Tkachuk behind them. They'll look to core players such as Tim Stützle to lead the way as they attempt to remain among the Eastern Conference playoff contenders.

A talented, swift-skating playmaking center, Stützle has been a star for the Senators since his rookie season in 2020-21. His 83 points last season led the Senators , marking the third time in four seasons he's held that honor.

Now 24, Stützle is approaching his prime. He will be expected to fill the leadership void. With his impressive offensive skills, he could be poised for a career-best performance this season.

Joining the Philadelphia Flyers late last season, Porter Martone had an immediate impact. He tallied 10 points in nine games, helping the rebuilding Flyers reach the playoffs, and finished second among their playoff scorers with five points in 10 postseason contests.

A big, strong power forward, Martone was chosen sixth overall in the 2025 NHL Draft. The 6'3", 210-pound winger quickly adapted to the NHL pace after only one season at Michigan State University.

Martone's size, offensive skills, and hockey smarts provided the Flyers a welcome boost of late-season energy and scoring. He must now prove he can handle the pace over a full NHL season as a first-line winger . If he performs as expected, he will be a contender for the Calder Memorial Trophy.

Now in his 22nd NHL season, Sidney Crosby is in his 20th season as captain of the Pittsburgh Penguins, making him the longest-serving captain in NHL history . It's another of the many accomplishments of the 39-year-old superstar.

Despite his age, Crosby remains among the NHL's most respected elite players. His leadership and all-around play factored into the retooling Penguins exceeding expectations and reaching the playoffs last season. Despite missing 14 games to a knee injury, he led the Penguins with 74 points in 68 games.

The Penguins hope Crosby will defy Father Time once again as they attempt to build on last season's performance. If he avoids injury, he could reach 90 points this season. That would vault him over Hall of Famers Marcel Dionne, Ron Francis, and Gordie Howe into fourth on the all-time points list .

In his second NHL season, Macklin Celebrini became a superstar. At only 19 in 2025-26, the San Jose Sharks' center finished fourth among the league's scoring leaders with 115 points, breaking Joe Thornton's single-season franchise record .

Many promising youngsters have been tabbed with the label of franchise player, but few have been as dazzling in such a short a period as Celebrini. A smart two-way play-making center who excels in big-game situations, he kept the rebuilding Sharks within playoff contention for most of last season.

Celebrini will be expected to lead the young Sharks into the playoffs. The gifted young center has set a high bar for himself, but based on what we've seen thus far, he shouldn't have much difficulty clearing it.

Acquired from the Toronto Maple Leafs at the trade deadline, Bobby McMann tallied 10 goals and 14 points in 18 games, providing the Seattle Kraken with a jolt of late-season energy. It wasn't enough to get them into the playoffs, but it holds the promise of what he could do for them over a full season.

McMann, 30, is a late-blooming scoring winger. The 6'2", 217-pounder tallied 20 goals with the Maple Leafs in 2024-25 and 29 goals between the Leafs and Kraken last season, earning himself a six-year contract extension .

That deal puts pressure on McMann to deliver on his scoring potential. With his size, speed, and work ethic, he could give the low-scoring Kraken a welcome offensive boost.

Last season was difficult for Robert Thomas. The St. Louis Blues center was plagued by injuries and was the subject of trade speculation. Nevertheless, he finished as their leading scorer , with 64 points in as many games.

Thomas indicated that he was never approached by management about waiving his no-trade clause. On Sept. 2, they gave him a vote of confidence by naming him team captain . With good health and the trade rumors behind him, the talented two-way center could have a strong bounce-back season.

The 27-year-old Thomas will once again center the first line between wingers Dylan Holloway and Jimmy Snuggerud. They should provide the Blues with a lethal scoring punch, giving them a shot at reaching the playoffs this season.

This season could be a crossroads for Nikita Kucherov and the Tampa Bay Lightning. The 33-year-old winger is in the final season of his contract and eligible for unrestricted free-agent status next July. The longer he goes without an extension, the more speculation there is about his future in Tampa Bay.

Kucherov is among this generation's greatest stars, sitting third in total points since 2015-16 with 1,041. He won the Hart Memorial Trophy for the second time last season and is a three-time Art Ross Trophy winner. Kucherov also played a big role in the Lightning's 2020 and 2021 Stanley Cup championships.

Coming off a team-leading 130-point performance , Kucherov remains the Lightning's offensive linchpin. Another high-scoring season will keep his club among the Eastern Conference's top teams. It will also improve his chances of a lucrative new deal with the Lightning or another team next summer.

The top prospect in the 2026 NHL Draft class , Gavin McKenna was chosen first overall by the Toronto Maple Leafs. Only 18-years-old, the young left winger is expected to play a significant role in the Maple Leafs' efforts to rebound from a disappointing 2025-26 season.

McKenna was a high-scoring forward with the Western Hockey League's Medicine Hat Tigers before signing last season with Penn State University. It didn't take long for the youngster to adjust to NCAA hockey, tying for fifth among US college scorers with 51 points in 35 games.

Projected as a highly skilled playmaking winger, McKenna could get some playing time alongside team captain Auston Matthews. If he adjusts well to the NHL pace, he could be on the path to becoming the Maple Leafs' next great star.

The Utah Mammoth are among the NHL's most promising teams. After several seasons of rebuilding, they clinched a playoff berth last season, throwing a scare into the Vegas Golden Knights in the opening round of the playoffs before falling in six games.

Dylan Guenther played a major role in the Mammoth's improvement in 2025-26. In his fourth NHL season, the 23-year-old winger enjoyed a breakout performance with a career-high, team-leading 40 goals . He also finished third among Mammoth scorers with 73 points.

Guenther is a smart, hard-working winger with terrific offensive abilities. Paired with rising star center Logan Cooley, he could reach 50 goals this season. He'll remain an invaluable core forward for the Mammoth.

On Dec. 12, the Vancouver Canucks traded superstar defenseman Quinn Hughes to the Minnesota Wild. Rookie blueliner Zeev Buium was one of the promising young players the Canucks received in the deal.

Buium finished the season with six goals and 26 points in 76 games. The 6'0", 183-pound puck-moving blueliner displayed plenty of potential as a future No. 1 defenseman with his strong skating, offensive instincts, and high hockey IQ.

Canucks management believes Buium is a star in the making and signed him to an eight-year contract extension worth an average annual value of $9.35 million. Given his impressive skills, he could soon make Canucks fans forget about the departed Hughes.

Last season was Mitch Marner's first with the Vega Golden Knights following nine tumultuous years with the Toronto Maple Leafs. His production dropped from a career-high 102 points in 2024-25 with the Maple Leafs to 80 points in 81 games with the Golden Knights.

However, Marner's production exploded during the Golden Knights' run to the Stanley Cup Final, leading all playoff scorers with 29 points. That performance silenced critics of his postseason record from his time in Toronto.

A creative playmaker with strong two-way abilities, the 29-year-old Marner is in the prime of his career. Now comfortably settled in Las Vegas, he could return to his 100-point form this season.

The Alex Ovechkin era will soon end for the Washington Capitals. As the 41-year-old superstar winds down his career, the Capitals made offseason additions such as wingers Alex Tuch and Jordan Kyrou and center Boone Jenner.

However, promising young players like 21-year-old Ryan Leonard could have the biggest impact for the Capitals. A physical, high-energy power forward, Leonard had a solid rookie campaign last season with 20 goals and 45 points.

Capitals management liked what they saw and signed Leonard to an eight-year extension worth an average annual value of $10.5 million. That new deal will pressure Leonard to meet heightened expectations, but he seems up to the challenge.

After winning the Presidents' Trophy in 2024-25, the Winnipeg Jets tumbled out of playoff contention last season. Among the few bright spots was the play of Mark Scheifele, who led the Jets with a career-high franchise record of 103 points.

Drafted by the Jets in 2011, Scheifele is their franchise leader with 961 games played, 372 goals, and 907 points. The 6'3", 207-pounder is a big, physical center with strong offensive skills. Now 33, he shows no signs of slowing down.

The Jets enter this season facing the prospect of trading superstar goalie Connor Hellebuyck. Scheifele cannot replace Hellebuyck's goaltending, but he will be expected to provide offense and leadership as the Jets try to bounce back.

Stats and award info via NHL.com . Contract and line combination info via PuckPedia .

articles.title: Pending NHL Free Agents 2027 Who Could Get Traded During the 2026-27 Season
articles.summary: With the way life in the NHL goes, it's never too early to start thinking about trades. While all eyes now are on Connor Hellebuyck and Dylan Larkin, looking ahead to next summer's free agent class gives us a look at a lot of other players who could be moved this season.
articles.body:
With the way life in the NHL goes, it's never too early to start thinking about trades. While all eyes now are on Connor Hellebuyck and Dylan Larkin, looking ahead to next summer's free agent class gives us a look at a lot of other players who could be moved this season.

We haven't dug into the science of it all, but players set to become free agents tend to be the ones most likely to be traded before the season is out. Whether it's because their team feels like they might not be able to keep them or a team is looking to sell before the trade deadline, players at the end of a contract make the most sense to deal away.

Even though the list of names of potential free agents is really juicy now, we know that a healthy number of them won't make it to July 1 without an extension in place. That's why we're keeping our list of names a bit more realistic... in most cases anyway.

Unlike his teammate Dylan Larkin, Alex DeBrincat is a Michigan native who would like to stick around with the Red Wings. Unfortunately for him, whatever happens with Larkin may dictate how the Wings' season goes and if it turns really bad, Detroit might be better suited to trade DeBrincat to cash in on a potentially juicy return.

DeBrincat was the Red Wings leading scorer last season with 41 goals and 44 assists (85 points). He's been an electrifying goal scorer throughout his career in Chicago and Ottawa previously and he's due for a big payday after this season is up as a free agent, whether he gets there or not.

No doubt that discussing an extension is on Detroit's to-do list, but they've been a bit, uh, messy this offseason dealing with Larkin, a search for a new GM, and trying to re-sign RFA defenseman Simon Edvinsson. One thing at a time, apparently. If time gets away from them, trading DeBrincat is a real possibility. And you thought Detroit's year couldn't get worse!

All eyes will be on Minnesota this season and not just because they're going to be a fun team to watch. They'll also be watching to see if/when Quinn Hughes gets traded for the second season in a row.

Wild GM Bill Guerin desperately wants to sign Hughes to an extension and considering how brilliant he was from the moment he arrived in St. Paul that's the right move. Then again, Quinn Hughes will cash in no matter where or when he signs and with his two younger brothers already playing together with the New Jersey Devils, it's impossible not to think that's ultimately where he wants to go.

Whether that means a trade to the Devils or to another team ready to make Hughes the highest paid player in the NHL the second he hops off the plane remains to be seen.

Then again, Guerin having all the time and ability to try and hammer something out gives him the advantage to either lock Hughes in for years to come or to trade him before word gets out that he needs to do that to ensure a whopper of a return.

It's kind of wild to think that Erik Karlsson is in the final year of his contract and that he very well could be a great deadline pickup for a team one more time in his career.

The 36-year-old three-time Norris Trophy winner is coming off a fantastic resurgent season with the Pittsburgh Penguins after finding new life in coach Dan Muse's system. There's no reason to think he can't continue doing that again this season and help spur Pittsburgh back into the playoffs again.

But should things go sour for the Pens, and the playoffs get out of reach, Karlsson would be immensely attractive on the final year of his contract. Yes, he's got a whopper of a cap hit at $10 million, but that's lower than it should be thanks to the San Jose Sharks eating part of that from the trade that sent him to Pittsburgh in 2023. A move at the deadline would make Karlsson's hit even more palatable and his skills and abilities would ideally bring more than a few suitors.

Although our lists like this like to focus on unrestricted free agents-to-be, it's hard to not look past some of the RFAs who are in awkward positions of their own with contracts coming due. None are more awkward than Columbus' Kirill Marchenko.

Marchenko had a thorny return to Blue Jackets training camp after he demanded a trade this summer. While he stated he loved hockey and enjoys being out there on the ice, when it came to doing all that in Columbus, he was a bit more evasive in answering.

It's hard to imagine things staying cool with the Blue Jackets and Marchenko much longer, never mind the rest of the season, and for a player of his skill and scoring ability, there's no doubt there are teams interested in finding a way to add him.

Marchenko will no doubt command top dollar for an extension and oddly enough, his RFA status has him in the driver's seat in a way to pick where he wants to go. After all, what team is going to spend assets to acquire him if he won't sign long-term there either?

A lot of how this season goes will determine what happens with a couple of the Boston Bruins top free agents-to-be and in Pavel Zacha's case, he could be in high demand if the Bruins fall out of contention.

Zacha has become a top two-way player in Boston and is coming off his most productive season as a pro. He had 30 goals and 35 assists (65 points) and set new career highs in goals and points. Since joining the Bruins, Zacha's offensive game has grown, and his defensive play has stayed steady from his years in New Jersey.

Zacha turns 30 in April and while that age can be a bit scary for some GMs, others see it as a sign of the player being their ideal self. For teams in need of a top six center with two-way ability, he'd make an ideal addition should things change with Boston in the standings or financially.

Some players have a way of finding their names in trade rumors all the time and Ryan O'Reilly is one of them. Ever since he landed in Nashville, there's been idle chatter about him finding his way to another team and now that he's in the last year of his contract with the Predators, that's not about to change.

What's working in O'Reilly's favor is he's already won a Stanley Cup and a Conn Smythe Trophy with St. Louis in 2019 which makes him an ideal player for contenders to zero in on for a trade. It also means O'Reilly won't just be cool with a trade to any team just for fun either.

O'Reilly is 35 years old and still playing strong hockey. His defensive game is still solid, he's good on faceoffs and he can still generate a ton of offense (74 points last season with 25 goals). If Nashville is out of playoff contention, it's hard to imagine he'll still be there by the trade deadline.

Another young player who's set to be a restricted free agent this summer is Rangers defenseman Braden Schneider. What's interesting with him is he was an RFA this summer and signed a one-year, $5.5 million contract. If it was a "show me" contract, it's a lot of money for one year to prove yourself which means teams ought to be calling New York about his availability.

Schneider is 25 years old and has been a fixture on the Rangers blue line the past four seasons. He's a steady 15-to-20 point a year player, can move the puck well and his advanced metrics are average-ish. You get the feeling the Rangers don't want to give up on a younger player but also lack internal options to push him and efforts to change that from the outside have fallen short.

Schneider could be an ideal change-of-scenery candidate in a trade, but if fortunes change for the Rangers, he could benefit from that. Then again, 2026 first-round pick Alberts Smits might be the guy that causes a Schneider trade to happen if he takes the blue line by storm.

Things haven't been looking positive for the Flames the past couple seasons and as they head into a new year, they could be looking at ways to tinker with the roster more, especially with forward Morgan Frost heading into free agency next summer.

Frost had his best season in three years last season with 22 goals and 21 assists (43 points) and should he build on that, it would help land him a raise on his $4.375 million cap hit this season. Since he became a full-time NHL player in 2022-2023 with the Flyers, he's been a steady 40-point per season player with the hope that his offensive numbers would improve and setting a career high with 22 goals last season might be an indicator of that happening now.

If Frost's offense continues to grow this season, the Flames will have a choice to make whether or not to offer him a raise on an extension or potentially have to deal him if he wants to test the market. At 27 years old, he's not likely going to develop as a player further, but if veteran savvy leads to more goals, he could be a sneaky addition for another team.

It's not to say that Casey Mittelstadt has been a perplexing player the past few seasons, but the offensive breakout we saw from him a few years ago with the Buffalo Sabres hasn't found its way to either Colorado or Boston in full. In Buffalo, he was nearly a 60-point player, but since then he's been around a 40-to-45-point player, still solid, but obviously not quite as potent.

Mittelstadt's skill is still very good. He possesses incredible hands and scoring instincts and a quick offensive mind. As he enters the final year of his contract with the Bruins, whether his future is meant to remain in Boston or to go elsewhere that his offense can better shine remains to be seen, but if the Bruins struggle this season, the chances of Mittelstadt going elsewhere in a trade would rise.

What's more interesting about his setup in Boston is that with J-J Peterka's arrival with the Bruins, Mittelstadt could end up on a line with fellow UFA-to-be Pavel Zacha, and that kind of arrangement could lead to both of them having career years with new contracts in the waiting. That would be a nice problem for the Bruins to have.

If it feels like we've been waiting a long time for Connor Hellebuyck and Dylan Larkin to get traded, imagine what it's been like for RFA-to-be Shane Wright. The Kaken more-or-less made it clear they were looking to move the 2022 No. 4 overall pick.

Wright has been a change of scenery candidate for about a year now (at least it feels that way) and after seeing his point total go from 44 two years ago to 27 last season under new coach Lane Lambert, it's more than a cause for concern for everyone involved. He was an elite skill player in junior hockey and had a strong first pro season in the AHL at 19 years old, but the situation in Seattle has been less-than helpful for Wright.

What Seattle would want in a trade and what a team would offer almost certainly differ drastically because Kraken management wouldn't want to have egg on their faces should Wright break out somewhere else. Barring a breakout to start this season, Seattle moving him seems inevitable if not overdue.

articles.title: Kean has an opportunity to make Italy history against Belgium in Mancini’s 2nd debut
articles.summary: Roberto Mancini is preparing for his second debut in charge of the Italy national team and centre-forward Moise Kean will have an opportunity to make Azzurri...
articles.body:
Roberto Mancini is preparing for his second debut in charge of the Italy national team and centre-forward Moise Kean will have an opportunity to make Azzurri history if he features against Belgium in the Nations League on Friday night.

Kean on the brink of Italy history ahead of Belgium clash

Kean is on an impressive goalscoring run for the Italy national team, with a career record of a goal every other game (13 from 26 caps).

BERGAMO – MARCH 26: Moise Kean celebrates scoring his team's second goal during the FIFA World Cup 2026 European Qualifiers KO play-offs match against Northern Ireland at Stadio di Bergamo on March 26, 2026 in Bergamo. (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

The Como centre-forward has also scored in each of the last six matches that he has played for Italy: Against Germany in a 3-3 draw back in March 2025, against Estonia twice on September 5 and October 11 last year, against Israel in World Cup qualification, and against Northern Ireland and Bosnia in the World Cup play-off campaign.

He is one of four players along with Roberto Bettega, Luigi Riva and Adolfo Baloncieri to have scored in six consecutive Italy outings.

If Kean finds the back of the net against Belgium on Friday, he will become the first and only player in history to have scored in seven consecutive outings for Italy.

ZENICA, BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA – MARCH 31: Moise Kean celebrates after scoring his team's opening goal during the FIFA World Cup 2026 European Qualifiers KO play-offs match against Bosnia and Herzegovina at Stadion Bilino Polje on March 31, 2026 in Zenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina. (Photo by Getty Images/Getty Images)

Kean's 13 goals make him the top scorer in the national team , ahead of Giacomo Raspadori with 11 and Nicolo Barella with 10. Mateo Retegui , who has not been called up on this occasion, also has 11.

articles.title: Leny Yoro earns first France call-up after Konaté injury
articles.summary: Manchester United defender Leny Yoro has received his first call-up to the France senior squad after Ibrahima Konaté was ruled out with a knee injury.Yoro, w...
articles.body:
Manchester United defender Leny Yoro has received his first call-up to the France senior squad after Ibrahima Konaté was ruled out with a knee injury.

Yoro, who had initially been with France's Under-21s, has been promoted to Zinedine Zidane's senior group ahead of the Nations League opener against Turkey on Friday.

The 20-year-old becomes the latest young defender to be given an opportunity by Zidane, who is preparing for his first competitive match since taking over as France head coach.

Konaté, who plays for Real Madrid , has withdrawn from the squad after suffering a minor knee problem and will return to his club for treatment.

Leny Yoro gets first France call-up after Ibrahima Konaté injury

Yoro's promotion comes just days after Zidane named his first France squad. The Manchester United centre-back was not initially included, with Liverpool defender Jérémy Jacquet among the new faces in the original selection.

The former Lille defender has already represented France at youth level and was part of the Under-21 group before being elevated to the senior side following Konaté's withdrawal.

France begin their Nations League campaign away to Turkey on 25 September before facing Belgium three days later. Zidane's side will then host Italy on 2 October before welcoming Belgium again on 5 October.

Yoro could therefore find himself involved in a demanding opening international window as Zidane begins shaping his France side following Didier Deschamps' departure.
